item.research_question: How can high-entropy alloy nanoparticles be synthesized rapidly and cost-effectively in a solid-phase without phase separation, and what are the underlying mechanisms involving laser interaction with precursors and supports?
item.material_system: CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticles encapsulated by graphene shells, synthesized on 3D porous laser-induced graphene (LIG) from polybenzimidazole (PBI) on carbon paper; also extended to CrMnFeCoNi oxide, sulfide, and phosphide.
item.processing_route: Dissolved equal-molar metal chlorides (CrCl3·6H2O, MnCl2, FeCl3, CoCl2·6H2O, NiCl2·6H2O) in ethanol/water; immersed LIG-coated carbon paper in solutions (1–20 mM); dried at 80 °C for 30 min; irradiated with Nd:YAG laser (1064 nm, 30 ns pulse width, 10 kHz repetition rate) under Ar atmosphere at scanning rates of 2000 mm/s and fluences of 58.9–96.8 mJ/cm2.
item.test_conditions: Electrocatalytic testing in 1 M KOH alkaline media; OER performance evaluated via LSV, Tafel analysis, and chronopotentiometry at current densities of 10–200 mA/cm2; stability tested for 428 h at 10 mA/cm2; temperature measured up to 2000 °C via infrared camera and simulated via ABAQUS.
key_findings: Production rate reached 30 g/h (specifically 29.6 g/h reported in text) under the current laser setup.
CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticles achieved an average size of ~15 nm (uniform between 0.005–0.015 M precursor concentration) and FCC solid solution structure.
Overpotential of 293 mV at 10 mA/cm2 for OER, outperforming commercial RuO2 (312 mV).
Tafel slope of 57.9 mV/dec for IE-HEA/LIG versus 83.1 mV/dec for commercial RuO2.
Exceptional stability over 428 h with only a 74 mV potential increase, whereas RuO2 disintegrated within 2 h.
Localized surface temperature reached 1960 K experimentally and simulated up to 2381 K with a cooling rate of 10^7 K/s.
Thermionic emission current reached 0.15 μA at 3 kV bias voltage under laser irradiation.
Mn content was lower than Fe, Co, and Ni due to partial vaporization (boiling point 2334 K) during synthesis.
item.mechanism: The synthesis proceeds via laser-induced photothermal decomposition of metal precursors and reduction by thermionic electrons emitted from the LIG support. Laser energy is absorbed by LIG, generating heat that conducts to precursors causing decomposition, while hot electrons reduce metal ions to atoms. Molten beads form above melting temperatures but are split into smaller droplets by laser-induced high pressure, followed by rapid solidification. The graphene layers bend to encapsulate the nanoparticles, preventing aggregation.
item.limitations: The text notes that the boiling temperature of Mn (2334 K) is close to the highest laser-induced temperature, leading to partial evaporation and non-equimolar composition (lower Mn content). Additionally, the disintegration of the carbon paper support was observed after 200 h due to rapid oxygen gas evolution, though less severe than with RuO2.
item.future_work: The authors state the technique demonstrates versatility for synthesizing HEA oxide, sulfide, and phosphide nanoparticles, suggesting further exploration of nonmetallic atom incorporation to induce lattice distortion and enhance performance. They also propose the method as an industrially viable solution for scalable manufacturing of composition-tunable nanomaterials.
quotes: The production rate reaches up to 30 g/h under the current laser setup.

The mechanisms of the laser solid-phase synthesis of HEA NPs on LIG supports are investigated through theoretical simulation and experimental observations, in consideration of mixed metal precursor adsorption, thermal decomposition, reduction through electrons from laser-induced thermionic emission, and liquid beads splitting.

The IE-HEA/LIG exhibited higher catalytic activity and exceptional stability toward oxygen evolution reaction (OER) over the commercial RuO2/C catalyst, manifesting the potential of the method to produce HEA NPs as a heterogeneous catalyst.
